title: HARVEST, a longitudinal patient record summarizer
research_question: Can an interactive, problem-oriented longitudinal summarizer built from clinical notes support physicians in reviewing complex patient histories without degrading task performance or efficiency relative to an established electronic record interface?
methodology: HARVEST extracts clinical problems from unstructured notes using scalable distributed NLP, computes problem salience, and presents visits, problems, and source notes through an interactive temporal visualization integrated with the institutional EHR. A formative crossover-style task evaluation involved 12 physicians completing four patient cases each under HARVEST and the institution's standard iNYP review system, producing 48 task questionnaires across 12 cases. The authors compared questionnaire performance, task completion, elapsed time, sensitivity analyses, and post-task usability feedback.

key_findings.finding: Physicians achieved similar task-questionnaire performance with HARVEST and the established iNYP system; the overall difference was not statistically significant.
Task-completion time did not differ significantly between HARVEST and iNYP, although HARVEST tended to take somewhat longer in the study.
Three quarters of participants said they would definitely use HARVEST again, and most participants rated its timeline, problem cloud, and note-access components as helpful.
HARVEST links salient longitudinal problems back to the clinical notes and time periods in which those problems were documented.
Simple frequency-based salience can be misleading because frequently documented concepts are not necessarily the most clinically important.
key_findings.section: HARVEST design limitations and future work

key_findings.finding: The evaluated version could include negated or provisional diagnoses as if they were ordinary problems because it lacked robust negation and uncertainty handling.
key_findings.section: Participant feedback / HARVEST design limitations and future work

key_findings.finding: The formative study does not demonstrate superiority over standard chart review; it demonstrates approximately maintained performance and efficiency despite participants being unfamiliar with HARVEST.

limitations: Only 12 physicians participated in the formative evaluation.
Participants were experienced users of iNYP but had essentially no prior experience with HARVEST, creating an asymmetric familiarity condition.
The experiment approximated clinical work with real cases and time pressure but did not observe physicians during ordinary real-world workflow.
The evaluation used patients from a single institution.
The evaluated timeline extended only two years, requiring users to return to the standard system for older information.
Problem extraction could surface negated statements and provisional diagnoses because robust negation and uncertainty processing was absent.
Problem salience relied heavily on documentation frequency rather than explicit clinical importance.
Complex records could produce cluttered timelines and large problem clouds.
The evaluated interface lacked convenient visit-level filtering and complete integration with other record components such as laboratory review.
raw_claims: HARVEST organizes longitudinal records around problems, time, encounters, and source notes.
The system extracts concepts from unstructured clinical documentation rather than relying only on structured problem lists.
Twelve physicians completed four patient-review cases each.
Overall task scores did not significantly differ between HARVEST and iNYP.
Task-completion time did not significantly differ between the two systems.
Participants generally expressed high satisfaction with HARVEST.
Most participants considered the timeline and direct note access helpful.
The problem cloud could contain negated conditions and diagnoses that were only considered provisionally.
Problem prominence was driven substantially by how frequently a concept appeared in notes.
The evaluation was confined to one institution and did not measure normal long-term clinical use.
HARVEST was intended as an adjunct to the EHR rather than a replacement for the complete medical record.
